paragraphs.text: This is [Dong Ding](taiwan-oolong:dong-ding) from Lugu Township in Nantou County, where the style takes its name, though the name is now used for the same style made elsewhere too. The leaf is withered in the sun and indoors, fixed, rolled into balls in cloth, dried and then roasted. This lot was roasted over charcoal, the traditional way.

It was made in 1996, which makes it thirty years old. Taiwan has a long habit of keeping oolong for years as [lao cha](taiwan-oolong:ageing), old tea. A tea set aside for keeping starts well roasted and dry, and the keeper roasts it again at low heat from time to time to drive out the moisture it takes in. No standard says when an oolong becomes old. Those who give a figure put it between ten and thirty years, so at thirty this tea sits at the far end of that range.

brewing.text: Ball-rolled Taiwan oolong takes hot water, about 90 to 100°C, a fairly generous amount of leaf and short steeps; the balls open slowly and give many infusions. Roasted Dong Ding takes water from about 95°C to a full boil. Aged oolong takes very hot water, in a pot that holds its heat, clay above all. Oriental Beauty is the exception and takes cooler water, about 80 to 95°C.

notice.text: A smooth, mellow, thick cup with little astringency, often plum or prune, sometimes something like medicinal herbs or ginseng, and an amber to red-brown liquor.
